blocks.x: This is February the 14th, 1970. Yes, Ray. And we're interviewing Tester Zardes, and we're in Preservation Hall. Yes, Ray. All right, Tester, well, one of the main things I wanted to ask you about was when you were playing in Over the Lake, in the early 20s or whenever it was, with Buddy Petit. Yeah, 19, 20, that's right. Okay, well, now, can you tell me everything you can remember about that, how you met Buddy and what way you would play and who else was in the band and generally all kinds of things like that. I mean, I'm really interested in Buddy Petit himself.

Well, you see, the way we started off, I was playing with a band out of, you know, around here in town until I got professional. I didn't get professional until I got with Buddy's band, you know what I mean? And Buddy had a pretty nice band. It was George Washington on trombone, and he had Faiso on drums. Then you had Edmund Hall on clarinet, and Buddy Petit was playing the trumpet. See? We didn't have, but there were six pieces, you know? Yeah. You know? And this boy, Hall, Hall was a pretty nice, you know, nice musician. I wish Buddy had really one of the best bands, you know? And after I got with Buddy, well then I commenced, you know, getting professional, real professional. See? Because after I got to be knowing, and I knew what I was doing, see? Because I was around here playing with these bands, and I didn't, wasn't playing like I should play. Well, Buddy Manatee, he was the banjo player with Buddy Petit's band.
Yeah.
And he showed me a whole lot, and from that on, well, I just went until I left Buddy. Well, I stayed with Buddy a long time.
How did you meet him? Can you remember?

Yeah, well, Buddy, he was raised up down my way, see, in the Seven Ward day. He was raised up, and after I heard that he had a band, so he came over and see me. Buddy, I mean, this Billy Marrera, that's my teacher, and he told Buddy about me. And that's where Buddy asked me would I join these bands, so I told him, yeah, I joined these bands, which I did. And before we left here and went to Covington, we was working at the St. Bernard Market, was playing there every Saturday evening, see? Around, say, about seven o'clock until nine o'clock, you know?
Yeah. Now, what can you, what year were you born?
Up on 1900.
1900. And can you, approximately how old were you when, when Billy Marrera came up to you and asked if you joined Buddy's band?
Well, I was around, say, about 17 years old.
Yeah.
Just around that age.
I see. Now, where was this, where is the Seven Ward?
The Seven Ward, that's between, uh, Espinade and Lichenfield.
Oh, I see. That's where Buddy was born?
That's where Buddy was born. Is the, I think it's, uh, 17, in the 1700 blocks in Atman Street. That's where he will live in that. Yeah. Between D'Oibany and Rowan.
I see.
Mm-hmm.
Now, what, when was it that he went over to play in Covington?

Uh, and Covington, well, you see, we had some jobs around here. We was playing at different halls around here. And, uh, then we, uh, we got a job to go to Covington. All right. So, after we left here and went to Covington, we stayed over in Covington for about, oh, must have been about five or six months. He was playing all around Covington and, uh, Burger Lucy or Beter Springs, you know. And all those surrounding places around there we was playing because Buddy had a nice name and Buddy was a real musician, you know what I mean? He knew what he was doing, you see? Yeah.
Uh-huh. Whereabouts, what sort of things would you play?
Like, uh, we all, we went all the way to Kentwood, Louisiana. We played all up in Kentwood and, uh, you know.
Playing for dances?
For dances, yeah. Yeah, dance music. That's right.
And, uh, Edmund Hall was the, um, clarinet player. He was, yeah. Now, can you tell me about how it was that he came to leave the band? Because he left the band there, didn't he?

Well, he left the band after we, uh, left from over there and came back here. We were still playing jobs around here and, uh, there's somebody sent for Edmund Hall. Some of them musicians from up the country, you know.
Yes.
And, uh, he told Buddy that he was going up, you know, going up there and try to make goods, which he did. Yeah.
He went, didn't he go to Florida then? Huh?
Florida?
He went to Florida. Some place. Maybe after, maybe a bit later.
I don't know exactly where, but I know to some way up north, just where he had went.
Um, well, um, now, can you remember George Lewis at that time?

George, I've been knowing George all my days. But George, like, uh, he wasn't over there at the time. We were over there, you know what I mean? But I've been knowing George. I used to play with George's band. We had a band with Chris Kelly. And, uh, the rest of the guys there, it was, I can't think all, all the fellas that, uh, we had at that time, you know. But I know Chris Kelly was waiting with us and the same, uh, Jim Robison. Jim Robison was working with us too in that band, you know. And, uh, we did good around here. We did nice. We had a nice band with Chris Kelly. Mm-hmm.
Now that was late then, wasn't it? That would have been later. That would have been after. That would have been after, say, in the mid-20s or something.

No, that wasn't that, uh, it wasn't quite the mid-20s. It was, uh, well, right after we left for our bodies. Yeah, around, oh, I think around, uh, I don't know, I just can't remember. Just, uh, the day so long, you know what I mean? The year. Mm-hmm. But I know Buddy stayed over there quite a while. And after we left them over there, that's when we came back here. And that's where we left for, you know, or this boy just sent for a hall to come up there. Well, after that time, my Buddy band was kind of going to pieces, you know? Mm-hmm. Well, I was playing with Kid Rene band, and I was playing with Jack Carey band, and, you know, Chris Kelly band. Well, just whatever band had to work, that's the band I'd work with, you know what I mean? Because sometimes I'd get messed up on my dates, well, I'd just go tell them, say, well, I've been taking the date for some such, you know, day, and that was it, you know what I mean? Mm-hmm. So, uh, it got to be all right like that.
Well, now, isn't it, isn't it the fact that George replaced, um, Edmund Hall when Edmund Hall left?

In Buddy band? Mm-hmm. Yeah, George played a while with Buddy band, see, but I was, I had left Buddy band, then I was working with Chris Kelly band, Ed Rene band, like I told you, and Jack Carey's band, you know? Yes. But George, he was still running around there with Buddy.
Yes, because I know that George was, he moved over there, his father was living over there or something, and he used to spend some time there in Madison.
Yes, yes, I remember that too, yes, that's right.
Do you remember anything about his father? No, I don't know.
No. Or his wife? No, no.
She's still living up, you know, around Vesaline.
Yeah, Vesaline and, yeah, yeah, yeah, I heard that.
Um, she told me about that playing over there, and she didn't remember, you know, who she even enjoyed playing with.
Mm-hmm.
Do you remember any of those other musicians over there in Manaville, like the Fritz brothers?
Yeah, I know the Fritz brothers, he was the Kranich player, you know what I mean? Fritz.
Isidore Fritz.
Isidore Fritz, that's right, he was.
What was he like?

Well, he was a pretty nice Kranich player, he was nice. Well, he, lots of times he'd come sit on in with Buddy's band, you know, with two Kranichs, you know what I mean? Just to get the swing of the music, you know? So after he got the swing, lots of times that Edmund Hall didn't feel like working, so he'd tell him to go in and make them jobs, you know? So he made a couple of jobs with Buddy, but he was a nice fellow.
Can you tell me anything about what he played like, or who he sounded like?
Well, you didn't know Big Eye Louie, I know you don't. No, that's right. Yeah, well he's on the order of Big Eye Louie. What he? Yeah, he's something like Big Eye Louie.

Sort of more classical kind of thing. That's right, that's right. That's right. Mm-hmm. Can you remember any of those other musicians over there, like they had Tommy Ladner there, I believe? Remember him? All right.
No, I didn't know Tommy Ladner.
He went up to New York, for sure. And then they had Bunkers over there sometimes, teaching some of those people.

Well, I weren't there when Bunker, when Bunkers over there. See, it's like I told you I came over here and I stayed over here. I didn't care about coming back because I was waiting with too many bands, you know? Yeah. And I was making more money here than I would go just waiting with one band over there, you know?
Yes. You know that picture taken with you and Buddy Petit over there in Mandeville?
That's Covington we're taking at you.
That's Covington. Can you remember the circumstances under which that picture was taken or, you know, anything about it to enlarge upon that picture at all? I mean, to describe the circumstances?

Well, no, it was no more than one day. We was, we was out, we was drinking and I used to drink then. And we had some fellow want to take, take the band's picture. So, we all agreed to him to take the picture. And we went out and it's a big place, you know, in New York. That's taken in the yard by the fence. And he's taking that picture. Even the boy that sings, I didn't know his name, you see. Yeah, they never did get his name. No, they never did get his name. And much as we used to be together, but I...

You don't remember where that was exactly? I mean, that was in Covington? That was in Covington. Yeah, yeah, I know that. Well, now tell me about Buddy's playing, because you know he was never recorded or anything. I remember that.

Buddy, Buddy's playing was great. Buddy wasn't, what you mean, what I call a high, you know, man that plays high. He doesn't play high at all. But what Buddy plays, he plays in the staff. You know what I mean? And when he play in the staff, I mean, so much melody and harmony through his music, you know what I mean? And he just, he just was wonderful. He got, he had a derby, a brown derby, and he put that derby on, you know, on his horn like that. And man, you talk about music, he'd make the music come out and then, he didn't have a loud band. The band wasn't loud. I mean, you could be playing and the people out there dancing, you could hear, you know, the footsteps, you know what I mean? Yeah, he was great.
Did he, did he have a good reputation? I mean, I mean, I mean, was he highly regarded by, by, by other musicians and other, and people who wanted him?

People liked it Buddy or plenty. They was crazy about Buddy. They was crazy about Buddy. They just say Buddy, sometime he just, you know what I mean, he just overdo it. Like any man would do when you get out with a bunch playing, he could drink, but he couldn't drink much, and at least a little bit of liquor he drank would, you know, would go to his head.
Can you, did, did he play anything like anybody you could mention, to give an idea of comparing him with anybody or anything?
No, there's nobody around who ever played like Buddy. Kid Howard used to try to imitate Buddy, but I mean, no. He never could. No.
Did he play anything like Bunk? Well, a little bit.

A little bit like Bunk, you know what I mean, but he's mostly in the staff. You see, sometimes Bunk used to go up a little bit, you know what I mean? Yeah. But Buddy never did go up there too much. He just stayed right down in the staff. Yeah.
Well, now, can you tell me about Chris Kelly and what he sounded like?

Well, Chris Kelly was a great man. He was great. But I mean, he's not to comparison, you know, with Buddy, you know what I mean? And Chris had lots of jobs around here, because I worked with Chris Van a long time too. And he had plenty of jobs and people liked it, Chris. Chris was a well-liked man. And he did nice around here, he really did nice.
And he was a good blues player.

He was a fine blues player, yes. He's another one, he had that derby, and when he started them blues, you know what I mean? He put that derby on there and make them the wah-wah, and you know, different tones come out of there like that. He was great. Yes.

Yeah. Of course, is that record which you made with Bill Russell there, with Kid Howard, where he plays on more on one of the numbers anyway, the Careless Love, which is supposed to be kind of close to the way Chris played that.

Well, it's a symbol. You see, you take Howard now. Howard is more closer to Chris than anyone of them, you know what I mean? Because him and Chris used to be together all the time. See, Howard was a drummer. See, and then Chris taught him a whole lot, see. And that's where he'd try to pick up Chris Kelly's style, you know. But he did pretty nice. He did pretty nice. He was good. He was a strong man, you know what I mean? Trumpets. He'd go up there and get them higher notes. Howard did. Oh, yeah. He'd get them. He had some of that Armstrong stuff.
Yes, yes. He got some Armstrong stuff. That's what he had. Sure did.
He was great. Well, can you remember any of the places, like when you were over here, like say, Chris Kelly,
or did you play with Buddy B.T over here? Did you play with Buddy B.T over here? Did you play with Buddy B.T over here? Yeah, I played over here too. Yeah.
Can you remember any of the places you played? Oh, yeah.
We played at the Corporate's Hall. We played at the Economy Hall.

We played up at the St. Sioux Hall. And most of all these places, that place they call the New Hall, that's down there. And, uh, lots of lone porters. We had lots of lone porters, and the Swells Club, the Lions Club, all them clubs, the Center Center's Club, we played all that.
What did, um, what did Buddy B.T look like?

Buddy was a fine-looking young man. He was fine. He wasn't a dog fella. He was in between, you know, but, uh, nice complexion. Real nice fella. And he was a slender, about a hundred and thirty-five, for the time.

Um, was he, what was he, was he, um, I'm just trying to, you know, get anything on counterpoint. You understand what you're talking about. Because there's so little, you know, that's not about him. Yeah, yeah, yeah. There's only two pictures of the livery to be discovered on him. No, no. I mean, I'm trying to think if you can think of any anecdotes or stories about him, or anything, you know, which comes to your mind, you know, to fill in something on that.

No, well, he was just a nice, nice fella. Oh, I can see about him just like I told you before. He'd get out and drink, you know what I mean, and drink a little bit too much and, you know, and that just, you know, but that didn't make the people dislike him anyhow, because he was always like it, regards to that, because people would buy liquor, they know he liked it, and they'd buy it and give it to him on the jobs, you know.
Who was, at that time, say in the 20s, who would you say was regarded as the outstanding trumpet player in the city at that time?

Well, that's the question, though. Buddy was good. Kid Rennie was good. Them two boys were real up to date. Chris Kelly was good. So, the comparison with them, they, all the people say that Rennie was, was the best, because Rennie went up there and he got them high and know he was something like, uh, this boy, Yvonne Thomas, you know what I mean? That's what, uh, Rennie were like. But, uh, they all were good. They all were good.
Did you ever play with Yvonne Thomas?
Yes. I played with Yvonne about, oh, I stayed there about, three years in Crowley, Louisiana. Oh, really?
Yeah.
You weren't there when he was killed, was he?
No, no, no.
He got killed, oh, that's a long time after I left. Yes.
He was killed around 31 or 32.
Yeah, well, I, well, I was back here then. I was waking out there on that boat there with the Pichon on the steam of capital at that time.
Uh-huh. Well, tell me about George Lewis at that time. What did, what did he sound like saying that?

George sounded good. George was really, I mean, I didn't know, George just mastered that horn and he had such a wonderful tone, you know? And, uh, everybody admired George's playing. And that's why George got to be known, you know, so much like he did because he had a nice tone and, uh, well, I mean, he was real active. I mean, active. He was great. Because any time, uh, you get on the, uh, I see one time we had a, uh, contest with two bands. Well, I was waking with, uh, Jack Carey band and, uh, George was with Chris Kelly band. And, but we had, uh, this boy, uh, Zeb Linares. I don't know if you ever heard talk of Zeb. Zeb was playing with Jack Carey band, which I wore too. And, uh, George, George was playing with Chris Kelly. But I mean, George played so much clarin'. That's how Zeb got, you know, just a bad feeling. He knew he couldn't come up to the stand like George did, you know? So, and, uh, everybody, well, don't worry about that. See, everybody's better and, you know, good and betters all over. Yeah, right.
Yeah. But he, did he play pretty much the same style then? Do you think George was his favorite later when he started to make records?
George? Yeah. George was on the same style. Yeah. George didn't change much at all.
Do you think he got any better?
Oh, yeah, he got better. Yeah.
George got a whole lot better than he was.
In fact, he always worked good. I mean, you know, the more you play your instrument, the more you get used to it, you know? Because you'll start his tone and fingering and all that, you know?
Yeah. Mm-hmm. When, when, when did you first, do you first remember meeting George?
When I first remember meeting George?
Yeah.

Well, I tell you, I was learning a bass at that time with, uh, Billy Moreira. And, uh, George played a banquet somewhere. I don't know where he played. I think it was at the Copper Raiders Hall. And, uh, Billy told George that, uh, I was, uh, learning bass on the hymn. So, George said, well, I know Chester Good. He knew all my brothers and everything, you know? So, that's where, he said, well, that's good. Chester said, keep up the good work. Just like that. So, I said, I'm a try. And I just kept on playing and playing until I got to be, you know, professional, like I tell you, when I went with Buddy. But I didn't consider myself a professional friend with them different little bands around here, you know what I mean? Until I got with a real organized band, you know what I mean?
Yeah. Mm-hmm.
Why'd they call this time? Not a night, everybody.
Um, so you remember meeting him like almost as a boy. Yeah.
Yeah.
That's right.
That's right. See, George, George around my age, you know? Yeah, well, the same age.
Yeah. Yeah, George around my age. That's right. Yeah. He used to live, in fact, right behind the Pope's Hall or Cooperative Hall. Yeah, Cooperative Hall.
That's right.
He used to live right, right by there. Yeah. Yeah.
Or St. Philip Street, I believe.
Yeah.
That's right.
Mm-hmm. Um, then I, you see, did you play with George? You played with George then when you made those records, but had you been playing with George much before that?

Yes. I had played jobs with George, you know. I didn't play study because I was busy with those other bands, you know. But I played lots of jobs with George when I couldn't play. Well, he'd get, there's a fellow by the name he called, Jose. You might have heard talking, Jose, a bass player. Well, he was playing.

Funnily enough, I heard of, you know who told me and mentioned his name? It was Emma George's wife. Emma, she, I was saying, who were the people that played over there, over the Lakers? Yeah. He said there was a man called Jose.
Jose, that's right.
That's right.
The old man.
That's right. I'd never heard that name before.
No. Well, I mean, he was annoying, you know what I mean? He played all right. He was...
Did he play over the Lakers?
Yes, he went over the Lakers with them, yeah.
Yeah.

And, uh, Buddy Van, before, I tell you, when they made us go over the Lakers, we was waking on them, on the steamer camellia. It used to run from, uh, Lellenboyd to Manville. We used to play on that boat, you know, it's a passenger boat going over to bring people like that. And we worked over there, and, uh, one of the guys from over in Covenant wanted, uh, to book the band. So, well, Buddy accepted that, taking it over to you. We didn't make much money, but I mean, we had so much fun, and, you know.
Now, can you remember exactly where it was that you played, where he did, where he was
in Covenant? The first place? No. No, I couldn't exactly say the first place, but I knew it was, uh, a club. I think that was the country club, they call it, out there. It was a nice, nice big place.
In Covenant?
In Covenant. Was that for colored people?
No, that's white.
For white? No, white.
Did you mainly play for white people, or did you play?

We played more white jobs than we did colored jobs. Really? Yeah. I'm surprised to hear that. Yeah, yeah. We had lots of jobs, like I told you. All around Campwood, Louisiana. All true that, you know, that I see that we played different places over there, and, uh, that's why a buddy got such a big, you know, a big name like he did. Bubba Lewis had always been Bubba. He used to play for the male. The male used to give dances over there all the time. Uh-huh.
Did they treat you nice?

Oh, yeah, yeah, them people. Well, I mean, you didn't have, uh, you know, I mean, none of that good liquor like they had, no, they got that, uh, what's called alcohol, you know? Well, that's the most, they were selling at that time, where they'd bring that stuff on there, and give it to the boys, you know? But boys treated you nice, they treated you like you was a musician. Oh. Yeah.
I mean, did they have any sort of racial, um, problems or anything like that?
No.
No.
No.
You take, you know, like that neighborhood up there now, you know, up around Barcaloosa and all, I mean, I don't know how you feel, but I wouldn't like to go out there too much.

No. Well, it wasn't like that at that time. Everybody didn't know their place, you know what I mean? You go in your place, and they go in their place, and that's the way they got along like that. It wasn't no humbug at all out there, because the white people were just as, you know, glad to have the colored band to play for them, and to have the white band, which they didn't have no white band out there at that time, you know? And that's why they used to catch Buddy all the time. And when we'd be waiting for the man, would he come get us? You know, they sent a big old truck to get us and bring us back. Go out there, feed you, and, you know, give you money. Last time, you, you, Bubba used to go out there and get money and wouldn't be working, you know? He said, well, I'm going out to Bubba Luce. He was staying in the club. He'd go out there and get forty, fifty dollars from the man all the time. He disliked the band so much, though, he would have did anything for the band. The man, that was? The man of Bubba Luce.
How much would you get paid for a job then?
Well, the job wasn't so hot. You'd make four or five hours, you know. Well, it was money at that time. Yeah, right.
Well, that's more money. Yeah, it was money. After you made those records with George in 1943, didn't you go into the Navy or something like that?
I went in the Army.
Right in the Army.
Right after that. That's right. That's correct.
Where did you get back to New Orleans?

Well, I stayed in the Army. I got in, it was about three years I stayed over there. And I got back around here around forty-six. I'll be a little before forty-six, but in that three years' time, you know.
Yeah. Did you play much then when you got back?

Yes, I played a whole lot when I got back, because when I first got back, this man of Gabriel, know that I got back and he came to my house and seen me, asked me if I wanted to work with him. He had a regular job playing at Mississippi City. That's, you know, I don't know if you know where that's at. That's way on the other side of, well, that's way away from Covington. But it's, I mean, it's a different route, you know what I mean? Well, anyhow, I played with him a long time over there, so, and that's the a long time, which was about a month. Then I got a, I got a telegram from Denver, Colorado, by a guy by the name of Floyd Hunt. He had a combo over there. Well, how he knew it, my name, I didn't know. He must have got it from the union. Well, all right, he sent me a telegram asking me if I wanted to join his band. And they were paying, oh, 175 hours a week. So, I asked at that telegram and told him that I was ready to come on out there, you know? So, after the boys in the band, Manna Gabriel and Hubert Moran, say, man, I wouldn't go out there if I was you, because if you're playing with some guys, you don't know. I said, let's don't know where you're going to get to know if you go to different places. So, I left about a week after, and I went out to Denver, Colorado, in a giant Floyd Hunts band. Well, he had a combo, you know? But he had a nice combo, too, really nice. So, they liked it, the way I played, and I stood with them a long time.
When would you say that the music here in New Orleans was, like, speaking, it's fine?
Well, you mean, since it was coming up like it is now, start clamming, you mean?

Well, if you had to, if you could put me back in the past at any particular point in time, to a point where I would, you would be able to tell me, well, you're going to hear the best music at this time than any other time, what time would you think, would you say that would be?

Well, during that time, there was music, that's what I say, it was a whole lot of music people was getting for nothing. I mean, the real Dixieland music. See, today you're paying for to hear Dixieland, but you don't get the original Dixieland music. See, everything then got more modern in Dixieland music. You understand what I'm talking about? Yeah. So that's, that's what, what I was telling a fellow the other day, when them bands used to be at the corners, and they'd all be tied up together, you'd really be getting some Dixieland music then. You know what I mean? And didn't pay for it, you'd stand there and listen to different bands, you know, you'd use your own opinion, and say, well that's the best band, you know.
Um, well what time, what date, or approximately what date would you say would have been a good time?
Well, say around the 20th, that's, yeah, around the late 20th. That's the time, that's right. Yeah.
Mm-hmm. Well now what do you think is it about the music that's, uh, that's not so good now?

Well it's not like it has been, cause I don't know the people, I mean, you see, everything changes. The music changes, the people change, see. People that's been hearing, uh, good music, I mean the older people, why do they, don't think, you know, some of them will tell you too, well that band didn't sound like they used to sound, you know, that band don't feel like they're the band, you know, different things like that, you know. But, uh, the people like it today, so you just got to go along with them, you know what I mean?
Yeah, but what do you think is, what is it that isn't as good now? What is it that's changed about the music?

Well you see, I'm gonna tell you what's changed about it, for one thing. You see, like, this man takes solo, that other man take a solo, that time there's no, everybody take no solo. You understand? Yeah. Alright, you take the rhythm section, there was a real background, a foundation, see. Alright, if the trumpet take a solo, trombone, and the clarinet would make a, a whiff, what you call, a riff in between, you know, behind him, to send him. And, uh, a clarinet player would take it, the trombone and the trumpet will take a riff behind him, you know. But, uh, today, they put an, alright, you take one, this man take a chorus, that other man take a chorus, and all right, that. Well that's, that's the difference in, in, in the music right there already, you know what I mean? Yeah. And then you take like a drummer. A drummer used to give you one beat. You see, when the band start off, he'd give you one beat, that's all he'd be beating, one beat. Alright, until, when that leader, trumpet player, knock, knock off, for out, well he's gonna give you a 4-4, what you call a 4-40. See, and that's 4-4, then he's gonna give you a 4-4 on that drum. And then he hit that, you know, that, you know, that, B-Guy plays something like that. You know those B-Guy's playing? Well that's, that's real old, old time. That's right.
Also they didn't seem to have, like in the old days they had, not far into something, they had the banjo more. Yeah, yeah.

Well I mean, last the band had banjos, and last them had guitars, you know. And when I, when I started coming up, well they was using guitars and banjos, because Buddy Manning, the same fellows you see on that picture there. He made that banjo himself, you know. And it was pretty, pretty, pretty good, you know.
Yeah.
So, that's where, well everything changed it, and then we couldn't, you know, do like, like they've been doing. See? Hmm? Yes, that's good.

How was it that you, you wrote, I mean, I ever once, I got a letter, I mean a letter came to Preservation Hall, that you'd written, saying that you'd, you'd heard, you know, playing there. George, I wrote to George.

Oh, you wrote to George? Yeah, I wrote to George Lewis. See, George had went to Japan, and, well, I, I was in the country at that time, and I bought that place out there, and I wrote to George, I said, well, I got kind of tired, I said, out there. I said, well, I'm glad George. So, I wrote George a letter, and told him, I said, in case you need a bass player, let me know, I said, I'm willing to come back to town.
Yes.

So, George didn't answer the letter, but Sandra answered the letter. She told me that she was glad to hear from me, and, well, she didn't know me, but she heard, you know, so much talk about it. So, I said, well, George is not here now, he's over in Japan, that's the time they left and went to Japan, see, see, but you'll be hearing more from us in the future, see. So, sure enough, I got a letter, quite two letters from Sandra, and she asked me when I were coming, so, I told her, I'll be most any time if I can, you know, get, you know, get a position, see, I said, well, all right, so, I stayed open that time around 65, well, I got sick over there, and, I went to a doctor out there in the library, so he said, I had to panic, he must rush me to the hospital here. I said, okay, so I had to go to the VA and get my papers, and after I got my papers, so, I got this 6 o'clock train that evening, I got here 11 o'clock at night, so, after I got off the bus, well, I rushed over to the VA hospital, when I got over there, they examined me, and they kept me over there, so, and I stayed there about, oh, about 28 days, and, uh, when I, when I got out, who I met but Cantrell, I said, Cantrell, I asked me where was I going, was I going back to the country? I said, yeah. They said, don't go back to the country, said, we need a man like you here, why don't you stay here? So, then he come and said, tell me about the job, you know, and everything, how it's good it is, so I said, well, I believe I will. So, and that's where, he asked me what I have to do to go back, I told him I had some cows and hoes and, you know, chickens, I said, well, I have to go back there and, you know, get rid of that stuff. So, he said, well, you go ahead back and write the man manure. So, which couple days after I went back, and I commenced selling all chickens, some of them I butchered and sold black market meat, you know, and sold chickens and different things like that. Now, the hardest trouble was me to get somebody to stay in the place out there. So, which I did, I got an old lady and an old man. I went about three, four places. I asked them if they wanted to stay, well, they didn't want to stay. So, it happened I went way around almost to St. Martinsville, and, uh, there's an old lady there, I know, I think so, and I asked them if they wanted to take you in my place. So, he told me, yes, do you want to stay, yes. So, you don't have nothing to pay but the electric and gas. So, I said, sure. So, they're still out there in the place now. So, that's when I came, came back here. Well, I came here one, one night, and I met Bill Russell. Bill had owed me $40 from that time. Really did. Bill said, Chester, I got some money for you. I said, oh, no. He said, yeah, I got some money for you. He said, I got $40. He said, I've been keeping that money for you all this time. I said, well, I only have interest on that money. And, uh, Bill gave me $40 right there at that gate there.
So, I... Did you go on any tours with, uh, with George, or, you went on tours, but did you go on any with him?

No, yeah, that's when George got sick. I went into Europe. See, I was on a tour with, uh, Billy, the D, and, uh, Nelson, and, uh, Faisal. I'm not Faisal, uh, Saeed. And George taking sick over there. We left George over there.
Was that in 60... do you remember the year of that?
That was 66, I believe.
Where was he, he took sick?
In Frankfurt.
What were the, what were the crowds like over there? The crowds? What were the people?

Oh, the people was great. Yeah, every concert we played, man, was, I mean, packed. Everything. And, uh, George has such a big hit over there, so, I mean, they've been knowing about George, they know about me, too, because, uh, they asked me, you Chester's in the house? I said, yeah. So, he went, got a book, and showed the same book, you know, showed me, and said, you can play a book. I said, yeah.
Yeah. But, I mean... Did you play in England, or did you just play in England?
No, we played in England. We played all over. Even, uh... You did play in England? Exactly, yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Can you remember what about in England did you find?
No. Very soon, so busy getting out there, man, so... I don't know.
How long were you on tour?
It was only about 30 days.
Was that the first time you'd been to Europe?
No, I was in Europe, and during wartime.
Oh, cool.
Do you think they appreciate the music more than in Europe, or? Than where?

Than here. Well, I don't know. I don't think so. But, uh, they like it. They're really crazy about it. I'll tell you, one night we played over there with, uh, George, in the same band, Bill and Denise. And, uh, where the women had his band up there, a big band, and they played one hour and we played one hour. And after they, uh, got off, we went on the stand. We started playing. And the people, they were so amazed at this Dixieland music, nobody wouldn't dance. They'd come straight all around the piano. And all you could do, hear heads, I mean, see heads and hear them feets, you know. And, uh, came and told us to say, you know one thing? They said, with that big band, where the women got, we're ready to hear this six piece band and hear that big band out there. I said, well, how you say that? I said, well, they got a beat. You got a beat to your music. I said, we could feel it. I said, but, uh, big bands, you don't feel it. Everybody makes, you know, different things.
That's right. That's really funny. I agree. Oh, yeah. Where was that? Do you remember? That was in Frankfurt. That was in Frankfurt?
Yeah. It was some kind of carnival they had over there at that time. Oh.
Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh.
Oh. Now you take another place where the people went wild over the music, over in Japan. Did you go to Japan?
I stayed in Japan three months.
You went there with the teeth.
Oh, yeah.

You went there with the teeth. Yeah. Three months we stayed in Japan. And the people were so amazed about the music, though. I mean, especially when we played, of course, the walk with the, I mean, the Japanese cry. It was so sad. You see, we had an interpreter there where he used to tell them what the way, what that music means and what we play that music for, you know? And after we'd play that, then we'd pick it up and, you know, then he'd tell them that's the way to do when we'd bring a bar that's to the graveyard. Yeah.
Did you ever play any instrument in the parade?
Yes, I played the bass horn in the parade. Yes, I did.
The bass drum?
No, the horn.
Oh, bass horn?
Yeah, yeah. I played the bass horn. I play it now, but I don't like that walk now. Yeah.
No, I got one. I got one in my face. Uh, tuba? Yeah.
It's called a sous-phone. Yeah.
Did you ever play that for dance jobs?
Yeah, I played it on the boat. I worked it on the boat with that. See, I used to double bass, violin, and the horn, see, on the boat. With Pichon bands. Yeah.

Mm-hmm. Do you think the music in New Orleans changed over the years? I mean, you've talked about how it's changed recently. Yeah, yeah. You know. Mm-hmm. But do you think the style itself has changed at all?

Well, I don't think so. You know what I mean? It's different bands, but it's different ways, you know what I mean? And it's a fool like, you take a rock and roll player, you put him with a Dixieland band, well, he just, you know what I mean? It's just something different altogether. Yeah.
Well, now, what about those early bands? Like, did you ever hear Manuel Perez? Yeah, yeah, sure.
They're great bands. What sort of style did they play? Well, mostly Dixiel's.
They're real, you know, Dixiel's.
But I mean, classic, you know what I mean? Yeah. Classics. Did they play, did they have the same kind of beat? No, just like I told you.
They didn't start off with that kind of beat like we started off now like that. All bands, they had that single beat.
You see one
Really? Can you think, now let's think of a tune. Down by the Riverside, you know that tune? How would they, how would they play it?
Well that's a single, that's one beat.
Yeah, well now can you sort of hum it how they would have painted before?

Well it's about the same, the same thing to play it, yeah. Just about. But I mean the time, you see what I'm talking about? Now of course we play it like old time, that one beat. See when we go out with that drummer, he'll give you that four on that, that, them last two choruses, see? That's right. You can't pick up that number special and play four four on that, unless, the boy just want to jump it, but I mean it doesn't sound right, you know what I mean? It doesn't sound like you can jump it. But if you play it at a nice time, you know what I mean? That's it.
Did you ever hear any of those real old bands, like the Robichaux band or anything like that? The Old Man Robichaux? Yeah, I was, yeah.
Well I see you take Robichaux band, that's mostly reading bands, see?
Yeah.

Yeah, all of them bands like that, they read music a lot, and then, you know, when you read music like that, you're going to read just what's on that tape, you see what I'm talking about? But today, now, you don't take none of these bands around, you read nothing on it, you see?
Did most of those bands in the old days, do you think most of the bands, do you think most of the bands were raised? Oh yeah, yeah, they were raised. What about Manny Perez?
Manny Perez had a good band, number one band.
Would you read it?
Yeah, yeah, he was a great musician, yes he did. Yeah, everybody read it. Robichaux too, Manny Joan Robichaux, they were reading bands.
Did you ever hear Bunk in the old days?
Yes, I heard Bunk, Bunk had a nice band, yeah, a really nice band.
What about Freddie Keppard?
Well I wasn't there when Freddie came, that's before my time. Yeah.
Yeah. Oliver, remember Oliver?
Yeah, yeah, remember Oliver, that was before my time.
Do you remember Louis Armstrong?

Yeah, well, Louis, well Louis, he's around my age too. Well, Louis and I, we were back at the homes a while, see we spent all the time in the homes out there enjoying life, you know. And, well he's been back there a good while, him, but I stayed a year back there. But, uh, after I got back there, I mean, the trees were so nice back there, but I used to come home every Saturday at 12 o'clock and go back, go back there Monday morning, you know what I mean? Seven o'clock, I had to be back there at 7 on a Monday. And I stayed back there all the week, but that violent Saturday, I'll come home again, stay sad Sunday and come home. Yeah.
I guess you never heard Bowden? No, no. Did you hear of him, or did you hear of him recently? No.
I never heard of Bowden. I hear lots of talk.
Yeah, what did you hear of him?

Well, I don't know what kind of great musician he was. Yeah, I said he was number one. What I mean they had, the boy was humming a song that he used to, uh, play all the time. What, I said, uh, what Buddy Bowden said, I think about, I think about take it away. That's what used to be his number, you know. That's one of his main numbers, and that's what they used to, the boy used to hum it all the time. I said, what was the thing I said, that's what Buddy Bowden used to play.
Um, did I have to play with, um, with Buddy Bowden?

Yeah, well, I played a while there, but we had George Washington. George was the main man. See, George Washington played with us all the while. It was just when George couldn't play while he did how well, you know.
He was a pretty good comment man, wasn't he? Was that, O.O? Oh, yeah.
Yeah, it was a nice time up here.
Mm-hmm.
And, uh, they had another fellow, he used to work with, uh, with Buddy, uh, Morris French, you know what I heard of? Yeah. Great man. I guess he's dead now, isn't he?
Oh, yeah, he's been dead quite a while. Well, he did nice.
He's a nice musician. Yeah, I think you made my new record. Yeah.
There was some story out there somewhere that there was a possibility that Buddy Bowden had made some records just for a home recording machine.
Well, I never had made any, all the while I was with Buddy, I didn't make no recording with Buddy.

There was some story, you made some in Thibodeau. That was in some book somewhere that nobody had ever found them, you know. So, nobody knows that they really did. Mm-hmm. Did you ever play with them there, or? In Thibodeau?
Yeah. Yeah, but we didn't make no recording, though. There was somebody just do like to come in here and steal it.
Yeah, I don't, I don't mean...
Yeah, like that.
I don't mean, you know, like a big recording company, but, you know, they used to have home recording machines, I think, in those days.
Well, it might have been, but we didn't know nothing about it. Yeah.
Yeah, I guess they never did, probably never were, eh? Mm-hmm. Did you ever see a picture of Chris Kelly? No, I never had. You never did find one?

Well, Chris was a fellow, I tell you, he didn't never care about taking those pictures. You know what I mean? Because, I mean, them guys, I don't know, there's something funny about them. A whole lot of people don't like to take pictures of the song, might break the camera and so forth, you know what I mean? It's something.
Yeah, they don't have time on them, eh? No.
I met his wife the other day, Edna. Yeah. And I asked about, did she ever get a picture of him? She said no. She said, Chris never did care about taking those pictures. Yeah.
I asked her that, too. She said she did see one once, but she's never been able to find one.
Well, Jack told me he had one, and I've been trying to get Jack, but I'll be Jack this, tell her I, you know, don't be. Yeah. Jack said he had one, he had his picture.
He said he looks a whole lot like one.
Yeah. Is that right?
Does he look like one? Yeah, he looks like Jack. Does he have the same building, you know, like he's like...
Yeah, he's built, yeah.
Yeah. Like a red ball. That's right.
Ah, well, that's about it.
It takes us about running out of it. Mm-hmm. How would you, just as a last question, how would you say George was, was rated, you know, his clownist, and you all inspired him?
Well, I mean, George had so much feelings when he was playing, you know, so much peps like that he, that emotions were, when he emotions, something coming out of that, you know what
I mean?
It makes you feel good to see him play and to hear him play. Yeah. Yeah, because I mean, what's coming out there is real, real stuff.
Was that, was that, was he more, was that more true of him than most other kind of players around him?
Yes, he was at that time, yeah.
In other words, you'd say he was one of the best.
He was the best ones around him, that's right.
Yeah. Because people like Big Eye Louie, I guess, had a bigger name in some ways.

Well, yes, they had a bigger name, even this boy that I was telling you about this, uh, boy was working with Jack, uh, Zeb Lennox, yeah. He was a pretty nice man, but I mean, he couldn't come up with standards with, uh, with George and those fellas, too. Yeah.
That's what I think, too. That's right.
Well, I guess that'll, that's just about to run out, so.
Yeah, okay.

segments.title: Joining Buddy Petit's band
segments.summary: Allen opens the interview asking about Over the Lake with Buddy Petit. Zardis names the six-piece band (Washington, Faiso, Edmund Hall, Manaday on banjo) and says Marrero introduced him to Buddy.

segments.title: Zardis's age and the Seven Ward
segments.summary: Born about 1900, he joined at about 17. He locates the Seven Ward and Buddy's birthplace.

segments.title: Months in Covington and Edmund Hall leaving
segments.summary: The band worked five or six months in Covington and nearby towns playing dances; Edmund Hall then left for a job up north.

segments.title: George Lewis, Chris Kelly's band and Buddy's later band
segments.summary: Zardis knew George Lewis but he was not there then; after Buddy's band faded he played with Chris Kelly, Kid Rena and Jack Carey, while George played with Buddy.

segments.title: Isidore Fritz and other musicians across the lake
segments.summary: Discussion of George's family and of Isidore Fritz, a clarinetist like Big Eye Louie who sat in with Buddy; Tommy Ladner and Bunk are mentioned.

segments.title: The photograph of Buddy's band in Covington
segments.summary: Allen asks about the Covington photograph; Zardis recalls a drinking day and a fellow taking the band's picture.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's trumpet style
segments.summary: Zardis describes Buddy's staff playing, melody, derby mute and quiet band, and compares him with Kid Howard and Bunk.

segments.title: Chris Kelly and Kid Howard
segments.summary: Chris Kelly as a well-liked blues player with a derby; Howard, once a drummer, learned from Chris.

segments.title: Halls played and what Buddy looked like
segments.summary: Halls and clubs where the band played, then Buddy's appearance and his drinking.

segments.title: Best trumpet players and Yvonne Thomas in Crowley
segments.summary: Buddy, Kid Rena and Chris Kelly compared; Zardis played about three years with Yvonne Thomas in Crowley.

segments.title: George Lewis's tone and the Zeb Linares contest
segments.summary: George's mastery and tone; a contest of Jack Carey's and Chris Kelly's bands with Zeb.

segments.title: First meeting George Lewis
segments.summary: Zardis recalls meeting George while learning bass with Billy Marrero, and where George lived.

segments.title: Playing with George, bass player Jose and the steamer to Covington
segments.summary: Occasional jobs with George, Jose the bass player, and the boat to Mandeville and a country club job in Covington.

segments.title: Playing for white audiences, treatment and pay
segments.summary: The band mostly played white jobs, was treated well, and was paid well; a patron paid Buddy generously.

segments.title: Army service and return to New Orleans, Floyd Hunt
segments.summary: After the 1943 records Zardis went into the Army for three years, returned about 1946, played at Mississippi City and joined Floyd Hunt in Denver.

segments.title: Best era of New Orleans music and how it changed
segments.summary: Zardis says the late 1920s were the best time, and describes changes in solos, rhythm section, drum beats and banjo.

segments.title: Writing to George Lewis and returning to New Orleans
segments.summary: Zardis wrote to George Lewis from the country, was answered by George's wife, fell ill in 1965, and returned to the city.

segments.title: Touring Europe with George Lewis, 1966
segments.summary: The 1966 European tour, George falling sick in Frankfurt, the crowds, and England.

segments.title: Frankfurt audience prefers the six-piece band
segments.summary: At a Frankfurt carnival, the crowd gathered around the small band rather than a big band.

segments.title: Japan tour and the funeral music
segments.summary: The Japan stay of three months, and an interpreter explaining the funeral music to the audience.

segments.title: Playing bass horn in parades and on the boat
segments.summary: Zardis played sousaphone in parades and doubled bass, violin and horn on the boat with Pichon.

segments.title: Whether the style has changed; the single beat
segments.summary: Zardis says the style has not changed; early bands played one beat, with four-four only in last choruses.

segments.title: Reading bands: Robichaux and Manuel Perez
segments.summary: Robichaux's and Perez's bands read music.

segments.title: Bunk, Keppard, Oliver and Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: Zardis heard Bunk, missed Keppard and Oliver, and talks about Armstrong at the Home.

segments.title: Buddy Bowden and possible recordings
segments.summary: Zardis never heard Bowden; talk of Bowden's tune, George Washington and Morris French, and rumored home recordings.

segments.title: Searching for a picture of Chris Kelly
segments.summary: Chris Kelly avoided photographs; his wife Edna and Jack say they have none or one.

segments.title: George Lewis's feeling and closing
segments.summary: Zardis calls George's playing emotional and the best around, then the interview ends.
